turns.text:
# ISO 27001:2022 Gap Analysis — Mid-Sized Fintech (Azure/SaaS, Hybrid, ~250 Staff)

## How to read the priority ratings

**P1 — Critical** (audit failure risk / regulatory exposure in fintech)
**P2 — High** (significant gaps, evidence typically requested early)
**P3 — Medium** (important but buildable on P1/P2 foundations)

---

## Clause-by-clause gap analysis

### Clause 4 — Organizational Context

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| No formal ISMS scope document | Policies exist but aren't consolidated | P1 | Define scope: Azure tenant, SaaS apps, hybrid workforce, fintech data assets. Document it. |
| Interested parties not documented | Likely implicit only | P2 | List regulators (FCA/PCI-DSS/etc.), customers, insurers, cloud providers. Document their requirements. |
| No context of the organization document | Absent | P2 | Produce internal/external issues register (can be a simple SWOT-style document) |

---

### Clause 5 — Leadership

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| No ISMS policy signed by top management | Some policies exist but scattered | P1 | Consolidate into a single Information Security Policy, get exec sign-off, publish it |
| No defined ISMS roles and responsibilities | Informal | P1 | Assign ISMS Owner (typically CISO or equiv.), document roles formally |
| Security not visibly on leadership agenda | Unknown | P2 | Establish a security steering group or add InfoSec to board/exec reporting cycle |

---

### Clause 6 — Planning (Risk)

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| No formal risk assessment | Absent | P1 | This is the heart of ISO 27001. Choose a methodology (FAIR, simple likelihood/impact matrix, etc.), assess risks against your asset inventory |
| No risk treatment plan | Absent | P1 | For each risk: accept, treat, transfer, or avoid. Document decisions and owners |
| No Statement of Applicability (SoA) | Absent | P1 | The SoA is a required document listing all 93 Annex A controls, whether each is applicable, and justification. Auditors will ask for this on day one. |
| No formal objectives | Absent | P2 | Set measurable information security objectives tied to business goals (e.g., 100% MFA coverage by Q3) |

---

### Clause 7 — Support

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Policies not consolidated | Scattered | P1 | Build a document management system (even SharePoint is fine) with version control, review dates, and ownership |
| No formal security awareness program | Unknown | P2 | Mandatory annual training minimum; phishing simulation strongly recommended for fintech |
| Competence records absent | Unknown | P2 | Document security-relevant roles and evidence of competence (certs, training records) |

---

### Clause 8 — Operations

This is where your Azure/SaaS/hybrid profile creates the most specific gaps.

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MFA only on admin accounts** | P1 — high fintech risk | P1 | Extend MFA to all users across Azure AD/Entra ID and all SaaS apps. Annex A 8.5 and 5.17 both apply. This will be a finding. |
| **Incomplete CMDB** | Jira-based, partial | P1 | Asset inventory is a prerequisite for risk assessment. Prioritize: Azure resources (use Azure Resource Graph/Defender for Cloud), SaaS apps (use Entra ID app registrations as a proxy), endpoints (Intune). Doesn't need to be perfect, needs to be defensible. |
| **Partial vendor inventory** | Incomplete | P1 | In fintech, supplier security (5.19–5.22) is heavily scrutinized. Build a register of critical suppliers: cloud providers, SaaS vendors, payment processors, data processors under GDPR. Document contractual security requirements. |
| **No formal change management** | Jira exists but informal | P2 | Formalize change records to show approval, testing, and rollback. Annex A 8.32. Your Jira workflow is a good foundation — add approval gates and security review for significant changes. |
| **Patching** | Intune/SCCM in place | P2 | Good foundation. Document your patching SLAs (e.g., critical patches within 72h), produce monthly patch compliance reports. Annex A 8.8. |
| **No formal incident management** | Jira exists | P2 | Add a security incident classification to your Jira incident process. Document roles, escalation, and post-incident review. Annex A 5.24–5.28. |
| **No ISMS** | Absent | P1 | The ISMS itself — the system of policies, processes, and controls — is what you're building. Everything else feeds into it. |
| Cryptography policy absent | Likely | P2 | Document encryption standards for data at rest and in transit across Azure (storage encryption, TLS requirements). Annex A 8.24. |
| Secure development | Unknown | P2 | If you build any internal software or configure SaaS pipelines, document secure development practices. Annex A 8.25–8.31. |
| Cloud-specific controls | Azure/SaaS | P2 | Annex A 5.23 (Information security for use of cloud services) is new in 2022. Document your cloud security policy, shared responsibility model acknowledgment, and exit/portability requirements for each provider. |
| Data classification | Unknown | P2 | Annex A 5.12–5.14. Define classification tiers (e.g., Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and label handling requirements. Especially important for fintech customer data. |
| Network and access segmentation | Hybrid workforce | P3 | Document network architecture, remote access controls (VPN/Zero Trust), and endpoint security baseline. |

---

### Clause 9 — Performance Evaluation

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| No internal audit program | Absent | P1 | You must conduct internal audits before certification. Build a simple annual audit schedule. |
| No management review | Absent | P1 | Formal documented management review of the ISMS at least annually. Minutes are audit evidence. |
| No metrics or KPIs | Absent | P2 | Define security metrics: patch compliance %, MFA coverage %, open vulnerability age, incident counts, training completion rates. |

---

### Clause 10 — Improvement

| Gap | Your situation | Priority | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| No nonconformity/corrective action process | Absent | P2 | When something goes wrong (incident, audit finding, near-miss), document what happened, root cause, and what you did. Auditors want to see this cycle working. |
| No continual improvement process | Absent | P3 | Document how you review and improve the ISMS over time. Can be as simple as a tracked improvement register. |

---

## Annex A control gaps specific to your profile

These are the controls most likely to be examined given your fintech/cloud/hybrid profile, beyond what's covered above.

| Control | Gap | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| 5.9 Asset inventory | Incomplete CMDB | P1 |
| 5.15 Access control | MFA gap, access review process absent | P1 |
| 5.18 Access rights management | No formal joiner/mover/leaver (JML) process documented | P1 |
| 5.19–5.22 Supplier security | Partial vendor inventory, likely no security clauses in all contracts | P1 |
| 5.23 Cloud services security | No cloud security policy documented | P1 |
| 8.5 Secure authentication | MFA not universal | P1 |
| 8.8 Technical vulnerability management | Patching exists but SLAs and reporting not formalized | P2 |
| 8.15/8.16 Logging and monitoring | Azure Monitor/Defender for Cloud likely partially configured — needs policy and review process | P2 |
| 6.3 Awareness and training | No formal program | P2 |
| 5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity | Likely undocumented for Azure/SaaS dependencies | P2 |

---

## Priority audit evidence to prepare first

These are the documents and records a certification auditor will ask for in Stage 1 (documentation review) and Stage 2 (evidence audit). Build these before anything else.

**Tier 1 — Must exist before Stage 1 audit**

The Statement of Applicability, ISMS scope document, Information Security Policy (exec-signed), risk assessment methodology and completed risk register, risk treatment plan with owners and timelines, and asset inventory (even if imperfect, it must exist and be actively maintained).

**Tier 2 — Must exist before Stage 2 audit**

Internal audit report (at least one cycle completed), management review minutes, MFA rollout evidence (Entra ID conditional access policies and coverage report), supplier register with security classification and contractual evidence, joiner/mover/leaver process documentation and recent access review records, patch compliance reports (at least 2–3 months of data), security awareness training completion records, incident log with at least a few closed security incidents showing the process working end-to-end, change records in Jira showing approval and security review steps, and logging/monitoring configuration evidence (Azure Defender for Cloud, SIEM if applicable).

**Tier 3 — Strongly recommended before certification**

Data classification policy with handling examples, cryptography/encryption standard, cloud security policy (covering Azure and each significant SaaS provider), business continuity and DR plan for critical systems, corrective action register showing at least one completed improvement cycle, and network architecture diagram (even a high-level one).

---

## Suggested sequencing (approximate 6–9 month roadmap)

Months 1–2 should focus on foundations: ISMS scope, Information Security Policy, asset inventory sprint, MFA rollout to all users, and appointing an ISMS owner. Months 2–4 should tackle the risk work: complete the risk assessment, produce the risk treatment plan, and draft the SoA. Simultaneously, formalize your Jira change and incident processes and build the supplier register. Months 4–6 should address the remaining P2 controls: awareness training, patching SLAs, logging review, JML process, and data classification. Months 6–8 should run the internal audit, hold management review, resolve findings, and engage a certification body for a readiness check. Months 8–9 is Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit.

---

A few fintech-specific notes worth flagging: if you're subject to FCA regulations, PCI-DSS (if card data in scope), or UK GDPR, there's significant overlap with ISO 27001 controls but also additional requirements. It's worth mapping those obligations into your risk register from the start rather than treating them separately. Also, your Azure footprint is actually an advantage — Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Entra ID, and Purview can generate a lot of your required evidence automatically if configured correctly.

Want me to draft the SoA template, a risk assessment matrix tailored to fintech, or a more detailed Azure evidence-gathering guide next?

## On your CMDB question — excellent instinct

Azure Resource Graph + Intune is a solid start but leaves real gaps. Here's what a defensible starting CMDB feed looks like for your profile:

**Definitely add all of these:**

Entra ID App Registrations and Enterprise Applications export covers your SaaS footprint — this is often the biggest gap auditors find in cloud-first orgs, since dozens of SaaS apps get connected without IT knowing. Azure Resource Graph covers IaaS/PaaS resources (VMs, storage accounts, databases, networking) but doesn't surface application-layer assets. Azure SQL / Storage / Key Vault inventory via Resource Graph or Defender for Cloud gives you data asset coverage, which is specifically required under 5.9 and 5.12. Your SaaS app list (from vendor invoices, procurement records, or a tool like Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps' shadow IT discovery) is essential — Resource Graph won't see Salesforce, Jira, or your payment gateway. Defender for Cloud asset inventory adds security posture context to your resources and is itself audit evidence for 8.9. Azure DevOps / GitHub repo list if you have internal development.

**Combined, these six sources give you coverage across four asset categories that ISO 27001 Annex A 5.9 requires:** hardware assets (Intune), software/cloud assets (Resource Graph + Defender for Cloud), data assets (Storage/SQL inventory + classification), and services/applications (Entra app registrations + SaaS list).

A practical tip: export all six sources to a single Excel workbook with one tab per source, add a "Master" tab that consolidates with a common Asset ID column, and label it "CMDB v1.0 — [date]". That's a defensible Tier 1 artifact even if it's imperfect, provided you document its known gaps and show it's actively maintained.

## Confirming your CMDB feed set

Yes — your proposed set is exactly right and will be defensible for audit. Here is the confirmed list with one addition and the rationale for each:

**Azure Resource Graph export** covers all Azure IaaS and PaaS resources: virtual machines, storage accounts, databases, networking, Key Vaults, App Services. Run via the Azure portal Resource Graph Explorer or CLI (`az graph query`). This is your cloud hardware and platform asset layer.

**Intune device export** covers all managed endpoints: laptops, mobile devices, hybrid-joined workstations. Export from Intune admin centre under Devices → All devices → Export. This is your hardware asset layer for endpoints.

**Entra ID App Registrations and Enterprise Applications export** covers all SaaS and internal applications connected to your identity plane. This is the most commonly missed feed in cloud-first orgs. Export from Entra admin centre or via Microsoft Graph. Covers both apps your developers registered and third-party SaaS apps using SSO.

**Azure SQL / Storage / Key Vault inventory** covers your data assets specifically, which Annex A 5.9 and 5.12 require you to identify and classify separately from infrastructure assets. Pull from Resource Graph filtered by resource type, or from Defender for Cloud's inventory view which groups by resource type.

**SaaS procurement and vendor list** covers SaaS tools not connected to Entra ID (shadow IT, legacy tools, tools paid by business units on personal cards). Source from finance/procurement system, expense reports, and DNS/proxy logs if available. Defender for Cloud Apps shadow IT discovery is excellent for this if licensed.

**Add: Microsoft Defender for Cloud asset inventory export.** This is the one addition I'd recommend beyond your list. It consolidates Azure resources with security posture context, flags unmonitored resources the other exports might miss, and is itself direct evidence for controls 8.9 and 8.16. Export from Defender for Cloud → Inventory → Download CSV.

Together these six sources give you coverage across all four asset categories ISO 27001 Annex A 5.9 requires: hardware, software and cloud services, data assets, and services and applications.

The practical approach is to export all six into a single Excel workbook with one tab per source, add a Master tab with a common Asset ID, Owner, Classification, and In-scope-for-ISMS columns, and save it as "CMDB-v1.0-[date].xlsx" in your ISMS document store. Document its known gaps in a brief accompanying note — auditors respond better to a transparent and actively maintained imperfect CMDB than a claimed-complete one that falls apart under questioning.
